title: Truist Small Business Banking ranks No. 1 in online and mobile banking
HSBC to sharpen focus on international wholesale clients in Türkiye
summary: HSBC Holdings plc has announced a review of retail banking and domestic-focused smaller and mid-sized corporate banking in Turkiye.
body_text: HSBC Holdings plc (‘HSBC’ or ‘HSBC Group’) today announces that it is sharpening its focus in Türkiye on clients with international and cross-border banking needs, as it undertakes a strategic review of its retail banking and primarily domestic-focused smaller and mid-sized corporate banking operations in the country. The review will consider all options for the retail banking business of HSBC Bank A.Ş. (‘HSBC Türkiye’) and its portfolio of smaller and medium-sized companies with primarily domestic banking requirements. No decisions have yet been made. The review does not include the remaining wholesale banking activities of HSBC’s Corporate and Institutional Banking business in Türkiye, where the bank will continue to support the growth of its international clients and local corporates with international needs. HSBC recognises the importance of Türkiye to its global network and will continue to have a strong presence in the country as it supports international companies investing in Türkiye and Turkish companies expanding overseas. The review is part of HSBC Group’s ongoing simplification globally. The bank's strategy is to increase leadership and market share in the areas where it has a clear competitive advantage and where it has the greatest opportunity to grow and support its clients. Media enquiries: Mina Sharma +44 (0)7837244371 mina.bharat.sharma@hsbc.com Ahmad Othman + 971 50 9002139 ahmadothman@hsbc.com Notes to editors: HSBC Holdings plc HSBC Holdings plc, the parent company of HSBC, is headquartered in London. HSBC serves customers worldwide from offices in 56 countries and territories. With assets of US$3,306bn at 31 March 2026, HSBC is one of the world’s largest banking and financial services organisations. title: Best AI sales signal tools for outreach teams
summary: Compare the best AI sales signal tools for outbound teams, and learn why the scoring model matters more than the feature list when picking one.
body_text: Outreach teams don't need more data, they need the right contact, at the right moment, with context that makes the first email worth opening instead of deleting. That's the real test for an AI sales signal tool: not how many signal types it tracks on a feature comparison chart, but how directly it connects those signals to personalized, sequence-ready action a rep can execute in seconds. What separates a good AI sales signal tool from a great one Three things matter most for outreach-focused teams evaluating options this year. First, how the tool scores signals, a generic industry model applied uniformly, versus one custom to your specific business and buyer history. Second, how quickly a signal becomes an action, a dashboard report someone has to remember to check, versus automatic sequence enrollment the moment a signal qualifies. Third, how visible the whole system is inside the tools reps already use, a separate login and yet another tab, versus built directly into Salesforce, HubSpot, or your sales engagement platform. Common approaches, and where they fall short Pure intent-data providers are strong on signal breadth but weak on personalization and action, you get a list of accounts or contacts, not a drafted email ready to send. Generic AI SDR tools generate volume but skip the signal layer almost entirely, producing more outreach without more precision, which usually just means more noise hitting more inboxes. Enterprise ABM platforms are built for account-level orchestration across large buying committees and rarely optimize for the individual-rep, sequence-level workflow that outbound teams need to execute day to day, deal to deal. UserGems' approach for outbound-focused teams UserGems combines Data Agents, which capture job changes, intent, funding, and tech stack signals across known and unknown contacts, plus your own CRM and call transcript history, with Intelligence Agents, which build a custom AI scoring model from your own sales history rather than industry averages borrowed from unrelated companies. For outbound teams specifically, Gem-E for Outbound takes that prioritized signal and drafts personalized emails, adds contacts to sequences, and researches closed-lost opportunities from past call transcripts, all flowing directly into the sales engagement platform your reps already use every day. The AI Chrome Extension puts all of this directly inside Salesforce or HubSpot, so there's no separate tool to check, no extra login, and no context switching before a call. Why the model matters more than the feature list Because the scoring model is built on your own historical wins and losses, not a generic industry pattern applied the same way to every customer, two companies never get the same weighting from UserGems. That transparency also means reps and managers can see exactly why a contact was prioritized, which signals drove it and how recently they occurred, and adjust when they know something the model doesn't, like a relationship history the data can't capture. Questions to ask any AI sales signal vendor Before choosing a tool, ask directly: does every customer get the same scoring model, or is ours unique to our data? Does a qualifying signal trigger a drafted email automatically, or does a rep still have to write it from scratch? And is the output visible inside our existing CRM and sales engagement platform, or does it require a new tab our reps will eventually stop opening? The bottom line The best AI sales signal tool for an outreach team isn't the one with the longest feature list on a comparison page, it's the one that turns a signal into a sequence-ready action automatically, without adding a new habit reps have to maintain. Teams making that shift have reported 2x SDR outbound capacity, backed by a scoring model that's proven not to lose a head-to-head data comparison against any competitor's data set. A short checklist for the shortlist When narrowing down a shortlist of AI sales signal tools, run each finalist through the same five questions in the same order, ideally against the same set of real accounts: what signals does it capture, and from known plus unknown contacts or only known ones; is the scoring model unique to your business or shared across every customer; does a qualifying signal produce a drafted, ready-to-send email or just a data point; does the output live inside Salesforce, HubSpot, or your sequence tool, or in a separate dashboard; and what happens to accuracy and adoption after the first 90 days, once the novelty of a new tool wears off. Vendors that answer all five clearly, with specifics rather than marketing language, tend to be the ones that actually stick a year later. Frequently asked questions What's a fair trial period to evaluate an AI sales signal tool? Thirty to sixty days against a defined set of accounts, with a clear metric tied to reply rates or meetings booked rather than just signal volume delivered, gives enough time to see whether the tool's output actually changes outbound results. Do AI sales signal tools work for teams without a large existing CRM history? Yes, though the scoring model improves as more historical win/loss data accumulates. Even early on, combining live signals with whatever CRM history exists produces more precise targeting than a purely generic, industry-wide model. How much manual review should a rep expect before sending a signal-informed email? The goal is a quick review and send, not a rewrite from scratch. If reps are still spending 10+ minutes per email after adopting a tool, the personalization engine isn't doing enough of the actual writing work. Should AI sales signal tools be evaluated separately from AI SDR tools? Yes, they solve different problems. AI SDR tools focus on generating outbound volume, while a genuine sales signal tool focuses on precision: making sure the accounts and contacts receiving outreach are the ones actually showing buying behavior, scored against your own historical data rather than a generic pattern. Can a small outbound team realistically adopt an AI sales signal tool without a RevOps hire? Yes, provided the tool is modular and largely automated, the setup burden should sit with the vendor's onboarding process, not with your team building custom scoring logic or wiring up integrations from scratch. ‍ No items found. title: System Connectivity for Homebuilders: Boost CX & Operations
summary: The Foundation buyer experience platform helps homebuilders sell more homes, more efficiently, to happier customers.
body_text: Most builders already have software. That isn't the problem. Problem starts after contract, when the buyer relationship moves across CRM, construction management, ERP, closing workflows, customer care, and a patchwork of emails, spreadsheets, texts, and phone calls. Sales thinks the handoff happened. Construction assumes the buyer got the update. Closing is chasing documents. Warranty later inherits the confusion. That's why system connectivity matters in homebuilding. It isn't just an IT project. It's an operations issue, a customer experience issue, and a visibility issue for leadership. When systems don't connect around the buyer-to-owner lifecycle, teams create workarounds. Workarounds create inconsistency. Inconsistency shows up as buyer frustration, slower handoffs, more manual follow-up, and weaker referral potential. The Real Cost of Disconnected Systems in Homebuilding The post-contract journey is where many builders lose control of the customer experience. The lead is sold. The home is in process. Internal teams are busy. But the buyer still wants clarity on what happens next, what documents are needed, what milestone was reached, and who owns the next step. In many organizations, that information exists. It just lives in the wrong places. A buyer's data may begin in CRM, move into ERP for contract and financial details, show up in construction management for build status, and later land in warranty tools for service. None of those systems is wrong. Each is doing its job. The failure happens in the gaps between them, where the customer relationship depends on people manually stitching together updates. Hidden cost shows up as manual work When systems stay disconnected, teams spend their day translating data instead of using it. Sales coordinators forward notes. Closing teams re-enter information. Customer care answers questions that should've already been addressed. Leaders get partial reports and delayed signals. That pattern has real operational consequences. Team Computers' analysis of the enterprise connectivity gap notes that disconnected systems can reduce productivity and decision-making efficiency by up to 30% when silos break communication between platforms like CRM, ERP, and construction management software. For a homebuilder, that doesn't look like an abstract enterprise issue. It looks like: Repeated buyer questions: Teams answer the same status questions across inboxes and calls. Missed handoffs: A next step exists, but no one has clear ownership. Inconsistent communication: One community gives proactive updates while another relies on reactive follow-up. Leadership blind spots: Executives can see job status, but not whether the buyer experience is on track. Practical rule: If a team has to check three systems and two inboxes to answer one buyer question, the builder has a system connectivity problem. Brand inconsistency starts inside operations Disconnected systems don't just slow teams down. They change how the brand feels to the customer. A builder may invest heavily in product, sales, and marketing, then leave the post-contract experience to ad hoc processes. That's where trust erodes. Buyers don't judge the company based on internal system boundaries. They judge it by whether updates are timely, next steps are clear, and issues are handled consistently. That's why the business case for system connectivity is broader than cleaner data. The goal is a connected experience across contract, construction, closing, warranty, and ownership. When that experience is fragmented, growth gets harder to scale without adding headcount and management overhead. Mapping Your Core Systems CRM ERP Construction and CX Most builders don't need fewer systems. They need clearer roles for the systems they already have. The cleanest way to think about system connectivity is to separate the job each platform is supposed to do. Confusion starts when leaders expect one system to cover every workflow, including the customer relationship after contract. The three operational backbones CRM manages leads, prospects, sales activity, and the early buyer relationship. It's where many customer records begin, and it's critical for pipeline visibility and sales execution. Construction management software runs the build. It handles schedules, milestones, field workflows, and production coordination. It's built for operational delivery, not for managing every customer-facing moment tied to that delivery. ERP manages financial and back-office operations. That includes contract details, options, purchasing, operational records, and other data that must stay accurate across the business. These systems are essential. None should be replaced just because the customer experience feels fragmented after contract. The missing fourth system What many builders lack is a dedicated customer experience layer after the sale begins. That's the fourth core system. It doesn't replace CRM, ERP, or construction management. It connects them around the buyer-to-owner lifecycle. That distinction matters. A connected customer experience layer should bring together: Buyer-facing milestones tied to operational progress Documents and action items in one place Shared visibility across sales, closing, construction, and customer care Consistent communication that reflects the builder's brand For teams evaluating integration strategy, it helps to start with a basic primer on understanding API integration . The technical connection matters, but the business question matters more: where should the information appear, for whom, and what action should it trigger? A builder-ready example of that approach appears in this look at a production-ready API strategy . The strongest architecture keeps each core system as a source of truth for its domain, then connects those domains into one usable customer journey. Why construction and ERP usually take longer The longest integrations are usually construction management and ERP. That isn't surprising. Those platforms often hold the most critical operational data, and they're usually the most customized by division, market, and internal process. Construction workflows vary by milestone structure, buyer update rhythm, and handoff model. ERP complexity often sits in contract data, purchasing, service records, vendor information, and ownership details. The right approach isn't to force a rigid template. It's to map existing workflows first, then decide what needs real-time movement, what can update on a schedule, and which actions should happen inside the customer experience workflow. Why Workflow Automation Outperforms Simple Data Syncs A lot of integrations disappoint because they stop at data movement. A simple sync can push a field from one system to another. That's useful, but it doesn't solve the daily problem most builders are dealing with. The core issue isn't whether a date moved. It's whether that change improved the workflow for the team and the buyer. Data sync updates records A basic integration might do this: Closing date changes in ERP: The date updates in another system. Buyer address changes in CRM: The record is refreshed elsewhere. Community assignment changes: The new field value appears across platforms. That's cleaner data. It's not a connected customer journey. Workflow automation changes behavior A stronger integration uses the same event to trigger action. If the closing date changes, the system should know what that means for communication, documents, internal ownership, and buyer expectations. In a connected model, one operational change can trigger: Updated buyer communication: The customer sees the new milestone or timing in the right channel. Internal task routing: Closing, sales, or customer care sees what now needs attention. Document readiness checks: Teams know whether required files or approvals are still outstanding. Visibility for leadership: Managers can see where the workflow slowed down. That's why workflow design matters more than sync volume. The best integrations disappear into the work. Teams don't want to think about where the data came from. They want the right information in the right place at the right time. A useful framing for builders comparing approaches is this guide to workflow automation software . A sync answers, “Did the record update?” A workflow answers, “Did the next step happen?” Why this matters more after contract Post-contract operations have more handoffs and more exceptions than most leaders realize. A single buyer journey can touch sales, design, financing coordination, construction updates, closing prep, homeowner education, and future service. If those transitions depend on manual reminders, they will break at scale. Automation should remove repetitive work so teams can spend more time on moments that require judgment, empathy, and expertise. In homebuilding, that means fewer status-chasing emails, fewer duplicate entries, and fewer situations where a customer asks a question the builder should've answered proactively. The payoff isn't just efficiency. It's consistency. Buyers experience one builder, not a set of departments. Anatomy of a Connected Post-Contract Workflow The difference between disconnected and connected systems becomes obvious in the sale-to-close journey. Before systems are connected, the buyer's information often starts in CRM, moves into ERP for contract and lot details, and then gets manually turned into customer-facing communication through inboxes, spreadsheets, phone calls, and disconnected portals. That's where updates get delayed, handoffs get missed, and buyers start asking what should happen next. That matters because the experience itself influences the business. Constellation HomeBuilder Systems reports that 73% of consumers view their home buying experience as more important than price and quality when making a purchasing decision. What the disconnected version looks like The common pattern is familiar. Sales closes the deal and moves on. Closing begins chasing signatures and documents. Construction has milestone information, but the buyer doesn't see it clearly. Customer care inherits context later, often without a full record of what the customer was told. That creates operational drag and customer uncertainty at the same time. A connected digital journey should feel more like one coordinated process. This example of a digital closing experience for homebuilders shows the type of buyer-facing clarity many teams are trying to create. Post-Contract Workflow Disconnected vs. Connected Systems Workflow Stage Disconnected Process (The 'Before') Connected Process (The 'After') Contract handoff Sales exports or emails buyer details to downstream teams Buyer record and core home data flow into the next workflow automatically Buyer communication Updates are sent manually by different teams in different formats Buyers receive guided, consistent updates in one branded experience Documents Files live across inboxes, shared drives, and separate portals Buyers access relevant documents in one place Milestones Construction progress exists internally but is translated manually for customers Operational milestones are turned into buyer-friendly updates and next steps Action items Teams chase signatures, selections, and checklist items through email and calls Action items appear clearly for both internal teams and buyers Closing coordination Closing teams spend time confirming who communicated what Shared visibility shows what's complete, what's outstanding, and who owns the next step Escalation risk Friction builds quietly until it surfaces as frustration or complaint Teams can spot stalled tasks and communication gaps earlier Builders don't need customers to see every internal system. They need customers to feel one coherent journey. In the connected version, CRM remains the sales source of truth. ERP keeps contract, home, and operational data accurate. The customer experience layer turns that information into milestones, documents, tasks, and guided communication that both buyers and internal teams can use. The biggest improvement is simple. Teams no longer have to manually stitch the experience together every day. Reducing Business and Brand Risk Across the Lifecycle The biggest risk in disconnected systems isn't technical. It's customer experience breakdown after contract. A buyer can be in one of the most emotional and expensive purchases of their life and still feel like no one is driving the process. That usually isn't because teams don't care. It's because communication, milestones, documents, and service activity are scattered across systems that were never designed to present one complete relationship view. Where risk actually appears Leaders usually see the symptoms first, not the cause: Poor reviews: The buyer didn't feel informed or supported. Warranty escalations: The issue may be operational, but the escalation starts with confusion or lack of visibility. Referral loss: A customer may like the home and still hesitate to recommend the builder because the process felt disjointed. Internal duplication: Multiple teams work the same issue because no shared view exists. The pattern is predictable. When visibility is fragmented, teams don't know what's been communicated, what the buyer is waiting on, or which action item is overdue. Visibility helps leaders intervene earlier A connected lifecycle view gives leaders more than dashboards. It gives them earlier warning. They can see whether communication is happening on time, whether documents are accessible, whether tasks are stalling, and whether a community or division is drifting into reactive mode. That makes it easier to catch friction before it becomes a reputation problem. Leadership view: The goal isn't to watch every task. It's to spot recurring breakdowns early enough to protect the experience and the brand. This is especially important after closing. Post-close communication, maintenance guidance, service requests, and ownership engagement all influence whether the relationship strengthens or deteriorates. Builders who treat connectivity as an operational risk-control layer tend to manage those transitions with more consistency. The result is fewer surprises. Buyers know what's happening. Teams know who owns the next step. Leaders get a clearer line of sight into where the journey is working and where it isn't. Metrics That Matter How to Measure Integration Success Most integration projects get judged on technical completion. That's too narrow. A homebuilder should measure system connectivity by whether daily work becomes easier, faster, and more visible. If teams still chase updates across inboxes and spreadsheets, the integration may be live, but it isn't successful. Start with operational proof The strongest metrics are the ones teams feel in the workflow: Fewer manual updates: Teams spend less time sending status emails or re-entering data. Faster handoffs: Sales, closing, construction, and customer care move work forward with less friction. Higher action item completion: Buyers and internal teams complete the next step with less chasing. Better document access: Fewer requests come in for files that should already be available. Clearer accountability: Teams can see what is outstanding and who owns it. For a broader scorecard, builders can pair those measures with customer-facing indicators. This overview of customer engagement metrics is useful for tracking whether buyers are opening updates, completing tasks, and using the experience as intended. Use business outcomes, not just system logs There is quantitative support for that operational focus. DataIntelo's home builder software market analysis states that builders using integrated software platforms reported an average 18–22% reduction in administrative time , a 14% improvement in on-time project delivery , and a 12% decrease in unplanned cost overruns . Those numbers matter because they connect integration to management outcomes, not technical activity. A practical executive scorecard should include a mix of workflow and lifecycle measures: Measure What it tells leadership Administrative workload Whether teams are gaining capacity or just moving work around On-time delivery performance Whether connectivity is improving coordination across handoffs Buyer engagement with updates and tasks Whether communication is reaching customers clearly Repetitive inbound questions Whether the journey is proactive enough Outstanding task visibility Whether managers can spot stalled steps early InetSoft's guidance on home builder CRM dashboards also points to Sales Velocity , Net Promoter Score , and Customer Churn Rate as important indicators for sales effectiveness and retention. Those aren't integration-only metrics, but they help leaders connect system decisions to revenue, loyalty, and long-term homeowner value. The best integrations become invisible Teams shouldn't have to think about the integration all day. They should notice that work flows with less effort. That's the test. Customer, home, community, milestone, document, closing, and service data should show up where it's needed without manual re-entry. Buyers should know what happens next. Internal teams should know what needs attention. Leadership should see friction while there's still time to fix it. Building Your Connected Customer Experience Strategy System connectivity becomes strategic when leadership stops treating it as a back-office cleanup effort. For homebuilders, the core question isn't whether systems can exchange data. It's whether the buyer-to-owner journey is connected enough to support growth, consistency, and brand trust over the next several quarters. Builders already have systems for leads, jobs, financials, and service. What they often lack is a connected layer for the customer relationship after the sale begins. What a strong strategy includes A practical strategy usually has four characteristics: Clear system roles: CRM, construction, ERP, and service tools each remain responsible for their domain. Workflow-driven integration: Data movement supports communication, tasks, visibility, and accountability. Leadership visibility: Executives can identify friction by community, division, or stage of the journey. Post-close continuity: The relationship continues through ownership, service, advocacy, and repeat purchase. A useful reference point is this perspective on the customer experience layer for homebuilders , which reflects the broader shift away from department-only software thinking. What to ask before approving the next integration Senior leaders should press on practical questions: Where does the customer journey break today? Which handoffs still depend on email, spreadsheets, or personal texts? What information should buyers see directly, instead of requesting manually? Where do leaders still lack visibility into communication and friction? Will this integration improve workflow, or only move data? The builders that scale well don't just connect software. They connect teams, accountability, and the customer experience across the full lifecycle. The goal isn't cleaner records for their own sake. The goal is a more connected experience from contract through closing, warranty, ownership, referrals, and repeat purchase. That's what makes system connectivity a business decision, not just a technical one. Foundation helps homebuilders connect the buyer-to-owner lifecycle without replacing their CRM, ERP, construction management, or warranty systems. It acts as the customer experience layer across existing tools so teams can reduce manual communication, improve visibility, standardize workflows, and deliver a builder-branded experience from contract through ownership. Learn more at Foundation .

title: Celebrating 25 years of visual search innovation
summary: Google Images is turning 25. Here’s a look back at some major milestones — and new ways to explore and create visual content.
body_text: Celebrating 25 years of visual search innovation Jul 14, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail We're celebrating Google Images turning 25 with a look back at some major milestones — and introducing new ways to explore and create visual content. Brad Kellett Senior Engineering Director, Search Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental This week marks 25 years since we launched Google Images , beginning the evolution of Search from a text-based experience to one that allows you to visually explore the world. To celebrate this milestone, we’re introducing two new ways to help you explore and create visual content — plus a look back at our major innovations in visual search. Explore images in a whole new way. Today, we're introducing a brand new browseable home for Google Images , featuring a dynamic, immersive gallery of images from across the web — updated in real time and intelligently tailored to your unique interests. As you browse and save ideas to your collections , they’ll appear as tabs above the main gallery, making it easy to jump back in and continue exploring based on what inspires you. This will roll out over the coming weeks on desktop in the U.S. in English. Sign in to your Google Account to try it out. Create new images right in Search. Sometimes, the perfect image is out there on the web, waiting to be found. But other times you might have a highly specific vision where an image doesn’t yet exist. To help bring those unique ideas to life, we’re bringing image generation directly into AI Overviews in Search. Using our latest Nano Banana model , this update transforms a simple text prompt into a high-quality, custom visual made completely from scratch, seamlessly bridging the gap between imagination and reality. Image generation in AI Overviews will start to roll out over the coming weeks in English, for all regions that currently support image creation in AI Mode . Both of these updates are built on 25 years of innovation to make the world’s visual information instantly accessible and useful. To see how we got here, let’s take a look back at some of the major launches that transformed how we search with — and for — images. 2001: Google Images When Jennifer Lopez’s iconic green Versace dress broke the internet in 2000, we realized that the standard search page at the time — a list of blue text links — simply wasn’t enough. People didn’t just want to read about the dress — they wanted to see it. So in July 2001, we launched Google Images, making it possible for the first time to search and instantly explore visual content from across the web. 2009: Similar Images The Similar Images feature made it possible to find pictures without relying on text alone. If you searched for “bow,” you might see images of hair bows and bows and arrows. By clicking the one you had in mind and tapping “find similar images,” you could see more of what you wanted without typing a whole new query. 2011: Search by Image We launched Search by Image to change how you navigate the web — moving beyond text to let the image do the work for you. By simply uploading an image or pasting its URL directly into the search bar, visuals became search terms. This allowed you to quickly identify the original source, track down where the photo appeared across the web or discover visually similar content. 2018: Google Lens in Search Google Lens makes your everyday life searchable, letting you use your smartphone camera to ask about the world around you. With Lens, you can identify objects, translate text and pull up product links in real time without typing a query into the search box. 2022: Multisearch in Lens Multisearch marked a significant step into the era of multimodal search. Now, you can search with text and images at the same time, like snapping a photo of a unique landmark and adding “what inspired this design.” Or taking a picture of a sleek dining table you saw on social and typing “coffee table” to find a similar piece for your own home. 2024: Circle to Search To help you search anything on your Android phone screen, we built Circle to Search . With a simple gesture — like circling, highlighting, scribbling or tapping — you can select what you’re curious about on your phone screen and get more information right in the moment, without switching apps. Circle to Search is available on more than 580 million Android devices around the world. 2025: Lens + AI Mode Last year, we brought together the multimodal power of Lens with AI Mode in Search so you can ask even more nuanced questions that require deeper reasoning. When you upload or snap a photo, AI Mode can process the entire scene. Using a " visual image fan-out " technique, it breaks a single image search into dozens of sub-queries to understand the full visual context and deliver relevant results. 2025: Search Live Building on our advanced multimodal capabilities, Search Live lets you share your phone’s live camera feed while having an interactive voice conversation in AI Mode — using video input to capture motion and the full context of your surroundings. It’s like having a video call with Search — great for everything from help in the kitchen to troubleshooting tricky equipment. 2025: Visual Results in AI Mode To make visual exploration feel more natural, we introduced an entirely new way to explore, imagine and shop using AI Mode in Search. You can describe exactly what you have in mind in a conversational way — like asking for "barrel jeans that aren't too baggy" — to instantly pull up a grid of visual inspiration and shoppable products. 2026: Circle to Search Multi-Object Recognition Circle to Search now lets you explore multiple objects within a single image all at once, using the visual image fan-out technique. You can instantly deconstruct and shop for an entire outfit or search multiple items in one scene simultaneously to learn about what you see. 2026: Intelligent Search Box With the new intelligent search box , you can now ask detailed questions about images right in Search and get a helpful AI Mode response.
